Data Appreciation · Week 5 · Title

Summarising: mean, median, mode and range

One number can describe a whole list — but which one depends on the data, and one outlier can mislead the mean.

Next Generation Genius · Year 1 · Foundation

Data Appreciation · Week 5 · Goals

By the end of today

  • Work out mean, median, mode and range
  • Use AVERAGE, MEDIAN, MODE, MIN and MAX in Sheets
  • Choose the right average when there is an outlier
Data Appreciation · Week 5 · Idea 1

Understand it

  • Mean: add them up and divide by how many. Uses every value — so one huge value drags it.
  • Median: the middle value when sorted (with an even count, halfway between the two middle ones). Not moved by outliers.
  • Mode: the most common value. The only one that works for categories.
  • Range: largest minus smallest — how spread out the data is.

In Google Sheets: =AVERAGE(B2:B9), =MEDIAN(B2:B9), =MODE(B2:B9), =MAX(B2:B9)-MIN(B2:B9).

Data Appreciation · Week 5 · Idea 2

Understand it

In the example, seven children get ₦200–₦600 a week and one gets ₦3,000. The mean is ₦700 — more than seven of the eight children get. The median, ₦350, describes a typical child. When you see "average" in the news, ask: which one?

Data Appreciation · Week 5 · Key words

Key words

Mean
total divided by the number of values
Median
the middle value when sorted
Mode
the most common value
Outlier
a value far from the rest
Range
largest minus smallest
Data Appreciation · Week 5 · Practice

Now you do it

  1. Work out the four summaries for eight pocket-money values by hand
  2. Check them with Sheets formulas
  3. Decide which average describes a typical child

Need a hand? Sort the numbers first; the median and mode become easy to see.

Done early? Add one more value that makes the mean LOWER than the median. What kind of value must it be?

Data Appreciation · Week 5 · Assessment

How you will be assessed

  • Weekly pocket money (₦): 200, 300, 300, 300, 400, 500, 600, 3000. Which average best describes a typical child?
  • Work out the median of 4, 9, 2, 7, 5, 8. Show the step that makes it easy.
  • Do the Khan Academy practice on mean and median until you get a streak of five, then say what you scored and one question that caught you out.

Your work is marked against the rubric, and you may be asked to explain your choices. Show your own thinking.
